# Offline scientific context: finite-temperature spin dynamics

This document provides the scientific background needed to interpret the
offline reproduction. It is a neutral summary of the physical contracts of a
finite-temperature spin-dynamics calculation; it is not a repair recipe.

## 1. Density operators and Liouville space

Spin dynamics describes an ensemble state with a density operator `rho`. A
simulation may store that operator as a vector in Liouville space, where a
matrix acts as a generator:

```text
    d rho / dt = R rho
```

The entries of `rho` are coordinates in a chosen representation. They are not
individually observable physical quantities. A different representation can
use a different coordinate layout while describing the same experiment.

## 2. The two Liouville representations in this task

The supplied Spinach snapshot supports two relevant representations:

- a compact spherical-tensor representation, which can exploit spin
  symmetries;
- a full Zeeman-product representation, which stores the operator space in a
  vectorized matrix form.

The representations are expected to agree on physical observables after the
appropriate conversion, but raw coordinate vectors and raw matrix entries do
not have to match. Scientific agreement must therefore be assessed through the
represented state and its observables rather than by matching array entries.

## 3. Finite-temperature equilibrium

At nonzero temperature, equilibrium is the normalized Boltzmann state generated
by the Hamiltonian. In Liouville coordinates its exact values depend on the
Hamiltonian, temperature, and representation. The representation-independent
requirement is that a generator which is claimed to relax toward that state
must leave it unchanged:

```text
    R_thermal rho_eq = 0
```

This is the same idea as a fixed point in a numerical dynamical system: if the
system is initialized at equilibrium, a relaxation-only propagation must not
create a new signal or drift away from equilibrium.

## 4. Thermalisation methods

Spinach exposes two finite-temperature routes used by the historical
validation examples:

- the inhomogeneous-master-equation (IME) construction, which embeds a target
  equilibrium state into a homogeneous generator;
- the DiBari-Levitt construction, which transforms a relaxation generator with
  a finite-temperature Hamiltonian propagator.

They use different numerical constructions, but they describe the same
physical relaxation process when their assumptions hold. Agreement should be
judged through fixed-point behavior and observables, not by comparing matrix
entries across representations.

## 5. What the reproduction measures

The public experiment uses a small four-spin fluorine system with chemical
shifts and scalar couplings adapted from a bundled Spinach molecular example.
It constructs the system through the normal Spinach initialisation path and
then invokes the ordinary finite-temperature equilibrium, relaxation,
thermalisation, and propagation interfaces.

The report is deliberately symptom-oriented. It records whether the result is
finite, whether the computed equilibrium remains stationary, and whether a
physical readout changes during a short relaxation-only propagation. It does
not provide an exact numerical answer or identify an implementation location.

## 6. References

- Hogben et al., *Spinach - A software library for simulation of spin dynamics
  in large spin systems*, Journal of Magnetic Resonance 208 (2011),
  <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmr.2010.11.008>.
- Levitt and Di Bari, *Steady State in Magnetic Resonance Pulse Experiments*,
  Physical Review Letters 69 (1992),
  <https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.69.3124>.
- Kuprov, *Defeating the Matrix*, Journal of Magnetic Resonance 306 (2019),
  <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmr.2019.07.031>.
- Spinach documentation, <https://spindynamics.org/wiki/index.php?title=Main_Page>.

The links are provenance references only. The benchmark must run with network
access disabled using the files supplied in the task payload.

% Modifies the relaxation superoperator to drive the system to the user-
% specified target state (inhomogeneous master equation formalism) or to
% the equilibrium state of the lab frame Hamiltonian at the temperature
% provided by the user (DiBari-Levitt formalism). Syntax:
%
%           R=thermalize(spin_system,R,HLSPS,T,rho_eq,method)
%
% Parameters:
%
%     R       - symmetric negative definite relaxation super-
%               operator that drives the system towards the
%               zero state vector; this may be obtained from
%               relaxation.m if inter.equilibrium is 'zero'
%
%     HLSPS   - lab frame Hamiltonian left side product super-
%               operator, available from hamiltonian.m (also
%               call orientation.m if necessary); this is not
%               required for IME formalism (pass empty array)
%
%     T       - absolute temperature, not required for the 
%               IME formalism (pass empty array)
%
%     rho_eq  - thermal equilibrium state, not required for 
%               the DiBari-Levitt formalism (pass empty array)
%
%     method  - 'dibari' for DiBari-Levitt thermalisation,
%               'IME' for the inhomogeneous master equation
%
% Outputs:
%
%     R       - thermalized relaxation superoperator
%
% Note: to work correctly, IME requires the population of the unit state 
%       in the state vector to be exactly 1. Spinach has no way of check-
%       ing or enforcing this requirement - take due care.
%
% Note: DiBari-Levitt method is computationally expensive, but tends to
%       work better than IME, particularly in exotic regimes.
%
% i.kuprov@soton.ac.uk
%
% <https://spindynamics.org/wiki/index.php?title=thermalize.m>

function R=thermalize(spin_system,R,HLSPS,T,rho_eq,method)

% Check consistency
grumble(spin_system,R,HLSPS,T,rho_eq,method);

% Get the unit state
unit=unit_state(spin_system);

% Choose the method
switch method
    
    case 'IME'
        
        % Apply IME correction
        R=R-kron(unit',R*rho_eq);
        
    case 'dibari'
        
        % Get the temperature factor
        beta=spin_system.tols.hbar/(spin_system.tols.kbol*T);

        % Modify the relaxation superoperator
        R=R*propagator(spin_system,HLSPS,1i*beta);
        
    otherwise
        
        % Complain and bomb out
        error('unknown thermalization method.');
        
end

end

% Consistency enforcement
function grumble(spin_system,R,HLSPS,T,rho_eq,method)
if (~isnumeric(R))||(size(R,1)~=size(R,2))
    error('R must be a square matrix.');
end
unit=unit_state(spin_system);
if norm(R*unit,2)>1e-10
    error('R appears to be thermalized already.');
end
if ~ischar(method)
    error('method must be a character string.');
end
if strcmp(method,'IME')
    if isempty(rho_eq)
        error('rho_eq cannot be empty for IME formalism.');
    end
    if (~isnumeric(rho_eq))||(~iscolumn(rho_eq))
        error('rho_eq must be a column vector.');
    end
end
if strcmp(method,'dibari')
    if isempty(HLSPS)
        error('HLSPS cannot be empty for DiBari-Levitt formalism.');
    end
    if (~isnumeric(HLSPS))||(size(HLSPS,1)~=size(HLSPS,2))
        error('HLSPS must be a square matrix.');
    end
    if norm(HLSPS*unit,2)<1e-8
        error('HLSPS appears to be a commutation superoperator.');
    end
    if isempty(T)
        error('T cannot be empty for DiBari-Levitt formalism.');
    end
    if (~isnumeric(T))||(~isreal(T))||(~isscalar(T))||(T<=0)
        error('T must be a positive real scalar.');
    end
end
end

% Returns the unit state vector or matrix in the current formalism
% and basis. Syntax:
%
%                     rho=unit_state(spin_system)
%
% Parameters:
%
%    spin_system  - Spinach data object containing basis 
%                   information (call basis.m first)
%
% Outputs:
%
%    rho          - vector or matrix representation of
%                   the unit state 
%
% i.kuprov@soton.ac.uk
% d.savostyanov@soton.ac.uk
%
% <https://spindynamics.org/wiki/index.php?title=unit_state.m>

function rho=unit_state(spin_system)

% Check consistency
grumble(spin_system);

% Decide how to proceed
switch spin_system.bas.formalism
    
    case 'sphten-liouv'
        
        % Unit population of T(0,0) state
        rho=sparse(1,1,1,size(spin_system.bas.basis,1),1);
        
    case 'zeeman-liouv'
        
        % Normalized stretched unit matrix
        rho=speye(prod(spin_system.comp.mults));
        rho=rho(:); rho=rho/norm(rho,2);
        
    case 'zeeman-hilb'
        
        % Sparse unit matrix
        rho=speye(prod(spin_system.comp.mults));
        
    otherwise
        
        % Complain and bomb out
        error('unknown formalism specification.');
        
end

end

% Consistency enforcement
function grumble(spin_system)
if (~isfield(spin_system,'bas'))||(~isfield(spin_system.bas,'formalism'))
    error('the spin_system object does not contain the required information.');
end
end

                % such because prod(spin_system.comp.mults) can be-

function dnp=dnp_freq_scan(spin_system,parameters,H,R,K) 

% Check consistency
grumble(spin_system,parameters,H,R,K);

% Damp unit state and check
R(1,1)=-mean(abs(diag(R))); Rc=condest(R);
if Rc>1e9, error('R must be non-singular.'); end
if ismember('redfield',spin_system.rlx.theories)&&...
           (Rc>1/spin_system.tols.rlx_integration)
    error('R acuracy too low, reduce spin_system.tols.rlx_integration');
end

% Preallocate the answer
dnp=zeros([numel(parameters.mw_frq) size(parameters.coil,2)],'like',1i);

switch parameters.method
    
    % Fokker-Planck path    
    case {'fp-backs','fp-gmres'}
        
        % Translate frequency offsets
        carrier_freq=-spin('E')*(parameters.g_ref/spin_system.tols.freeg)*spin_system.inter.magnet;
        parameters.mw_frq=carrier_freq+parameters.mw_frq;
        
        % Get problem dimensions

% Adds phenomenological pumping terms to the relaxation superoperator 
% to enable approximate simulation of CIDNP, PHIP and DNP type effects. 
% Syntax:
%
%                  R=magpump(spin_system,R,rho,rate)
%
% Parameters:
%
%    R    - relaxation superoperator, from relaxation()
%
%    rho  - the state to be pumped, from state()
%
%    rate - pumping rate, Hz
%
% Outputs:
%
%    R    - modified relaxation superoperator
%
% Note: for the pumping to work correctly, the unit state population 
%       (first element) in the state vector that R will be acting on 
%        must be set to 1.
%
% Note: this function is only available in sphten-liouv formalism, and
%       may be called repeatedly if multiple states are pumped.
%
% i.kuprov@soton.ac.uk
%
% <https://spindynamics.org/wiki/index.php?title=magpump.m>

function R=magpump(spin_system,R,rho,rate)

% Check consisttency
grumble(spin_system,R,rho,rate);

% Add pumping as a coupling to unit state
R(:,1)=R(:,1)+rate*rho;

end

% Consistency enforcement
function grumble(spin_system,R,rho,rate)
if (~isnumeric(R))||(~ismatrix(R))
    error('R must be a matrix.');
end
if (~isnumeric(rho))||(~iscolumn(rho))
    error('rho must be a column vector.');
end
if (~isnumeric(rate))||(~real(rate))||(~isscalar(rate))
    error('rate must be a real scalar.');
end
if ~ismember(spin_system.bas.formalism,{'sphten-liouv'})
    error('this function is only available in sphten-liouv formalism.');
end
end

Both symptoms came from a single broken physical contract: **the identity ("unit state") convention in Liouville space**.

1. **`unit_state.m` (zeeman-liouv) returned a 2-norm-normalised `vec(I)`**, i.e. `vec(I)/√d`, while every other part of the library (`state.m`, `equilibrium.m`, `thermalize.m`, the `jdnp`/CIDNP projector constructions) treats the unit state as *the unit operator*, whose inner product with a unit-trace density matrix is 1.
